meta.title: MoFT Reporting Solution — Testing & Validation Report
meta.footer_note: Compiled from QA status reports 1–4 October 2026 · Dev environment · Draft for internal review before client distribution

summary_callout: The largest single contributor to the client's experience is not a report defect. The database refresh is not running as expected, so the client environment can serve figures that lag the source. Reports computed correctly from stale inputs appear wrong when compared against live network data. A P1 has been raised and a minimum daily refresh cadence proposed.
defect_callout: Data accuracy and completeness together account for 59% of all defects. That concentration is the argument for automation: these are exactly the checks a machine performs identically across every country, and the ones manual sampling misses first.

sections.title: Testing strategy
sections.lead: Risk-based manual validation in this cycle, with automation being stood up in parallel. Three independent layers were applied to each report:

rows: Slide structure, labels, charts render, no raw N/A placeholders
Report figures reconciled value by value
Published trade figures compared against independent sources
Narrative wording, interpretation, phrasing of derived figures

sections.title: Scope and countries validated
sections.lead: Countries were selected to span distinct risk profiles rather than by volume.

rows: China, India, Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Andorra, Antigua & Barbuda, Bahamas, Barbados, St Kitts & Nevis
Türkiye, India, Georgia, Australia, Mauritius, Indonesia
China, Switzerland, Jordan, Armenia, India, Ireland, UK, Saudi Arabia, USA, Egypt

items: Large trading partners — high data volume; exercises aggregation, ranking and chart density at scale.

Small and micro economies — sparse data exposes rounding on small values, single-product charts, missing-data placeholders and extreme percentage swings. Most defects in this cycle came from this group.
CEPA signatory states — required for the CEPA report type.
Services-heavy economies — chosen for Trade in Services, where WTO and UNCTAD cross-checks are meaningful.

blocks.text: All validation in this period was manual. No automated regression coverage existed for the report types at the start of the cycle. This is stated plainly because it is the root cause of the defect escapes the client observed: with manual-only verification, coverage is limited to the sample a person can check in a day, and a fix in one country is not automatically re-verified across the others.

items: Scope of first suite — highest-risk data checks across all four report types: totals, percentages, year-on-year comparisons, chart values, and missing or unexpected data.
Daily scheduled regression with results pushed to Teams or email, so failures are visible the morning they occur rather than when the client finds them.
Dependency — coverage depends on receiving complete report data dumps by country and year, and on confirming the expected calculation rules.

blocks.text: Reporting commitment. Automated coverage will be reported as checks actually executed, broken down by report type — not as a single percentage. Where a report type has no automated coverage, that will be stated rather than averaged away.

sections.title: Environment and system constraints
sections.lead: These limited what could be validated in the period. Each is tracked.

rows: Client environment can serve figures that lag the source. Reports computed correctly from stale inputs appear wrong against live network data.
P1 raised Minimum daily refresh proposed
Report generation API not available to QA
The API collection supplied covers the AI agent, not report generation. API-level automation cannot begin until the correct collection is provided.
CEPA data accuracy could not initially be reconciled. Extracting the logic from application code was assessed as too slow to be practical.
Partner-country and signing-date data, and business licence and investment data, remain unverified.
Prevents comparison at scale. Countries and periods outside the manual sample are untested.
WTO and UNCTAD publish differing values for the same measures, producing variances that are not product defects.
Extreme percentage values calculate correctly but have no agreed display convention, so “correct” cannot be defined for test purposes.

items: Each report is generated through the product, exactly as the client would generate it.
Figures are extracted and reconciled against custom SQL run directly on the source database.
For Trade in Services, values are additionally cross-checked against published WTO data.
Formatting is compared slide by slide against the client-provided sample reports.
Narrative content is reviewed separately by a subject-matter reviewer.
Sample-based, not exhaustive. The product can generate reports for far more countries and periods than were tested.
Reconciliation is only as authoritative as the query. Where QA wrote the comparison SQL, a shared misunderstanding of the business rule would pass validation on both sides.
CEPA slides 2 and 15 carry no data validation at all — formatting only.
Point-in-time. Validation reflects the data present at execution.

sections.title: AI-related limitations and considerations
sections.lead: Characteristics of the approach, not defects to be fixed one by one.

items: Wording is not deterministic. The same inputs can produce differently worded narrative between generations. A fix verified in one generated report is not automatically present in the next.
House style is not guaranteed. Generated text may not match the phrasing conventions the client uses in their own publications.
Interpretation of derived figures. A correctly calculated value can be described in a way that overstates its scope.
Intermittency complicates verification. Non-deterministic output means an issue that cannot be reproduced on retest has not necessarily been fixed.

blocks.text: Recommendation. Narrative sections that must carry exact, auditable wording should be driven by templates with data substitution rather than free generation.

items: Fixes were released without regression coverage. Verifying a fix in one country said nothing about the others. The client found the gap before we did.
Stale data was read as report defects. Diagnostic effort went to report logic that was not at fault.
Validation was blocked on inputs owned by others — source queries, data dumps, the report API.

rows: Fix the database refresh; minimum daily cadence with monitoring and alerting on failure
Provide the report generation API collection
Deliver report data dumps by country and year; confirm expected calculation rules
Complete the first regression suite across all four report types
Daily scheduled regression with results pushed to Teams or email
Release control: MR verification on dev → release notes → branch strategy → CI/CD
Incident handling: hotfix policy and documented rollback procedure
Client decisions on extreme percentage display and authoritative source per measure
Test summary included with every major release

blocks.text: Residual risk if items 1–3 remain open. Automation cannot reach meaningful coverage without the API collection and the data dumps, and no amount of testing compensates for a stale database in the client environment.
